source.title: Benchmarking down-scaled (not so large) pre-trained language models
source.authors: M. Aßenmacher; Patrick Schulze; C. Heumann

page_placements.theme: Architecture shape and component allocation affect downstream quality

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies down-scaled Transformer size and shape and measures WikiText-103 validation loss and GLUE performance, but does not fit Kaplan-style scaling laws or use the same large-scale setup.
record.gate_note: The study measures validation loss over size and shape, and downstream GLUE scores over size and shape. It does not fit power laws or report exponents. Experiments varying training steps and batch size are not rows for V3 because they do not find a fixed-compute, loss-minimising parameter/token allocation trend.
record.test_reason: Down-scaled BERT-, RoBERTa- and GPT-2-style models are pre-trained on WikiText-103. The study reports how validation loss changes with shape at fixed size (Fig. 3, Table 7), bearing on V4. It also reports how GLUE-Large changes with size and with validation loss (Tables 1, 4–6, Observation 5), bearing on V6. It never fits a power law. Its loss-vs-size results (two or three points per comparison) cannot test the V1 form.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors' headline finding is that the MLM+NSP (BERT-style) objective consistently beats MLM and LM. They also conclude that model size is the key factor: both validation loss and GLUE improve with size at small extra training time, so compute should go mainly to size rather than more steps. They find that varied shapes can reach similar GLUE if multiple dimensions are scaled, and that validation loss is not necessarily a good indicator of fine-tuned performance.
record.recipe_differences: Uses down-scaled BERT-, RoBERTa- and GPT-2-style systems trained on WikiText-103; studies validation loss and GLUE performance rather than fitting the original large-scale language-model scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Pre-training objective and architecture shape affect GLUE performance. Validation loss and downstream performance can move differently across width and depth changes.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal size, fine-tuned GLUE-Large depends on shape and attention heads differently by objective. Wide A=8 is 78.4 vs balanced 78.6 (BERT), 66.0 vs 63.8 (GPT-2) and 70.9 vs 75.0 (RoBERTa).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream fine-tuned performance at fixed parameter count depends on model shape, and the dependence differs by pre-training objective.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a fixed wall-clock budget, the 7.1M system reaches lower loss than the 3.5M system at every point (Fig. 3). Halving steps hurts GLUE more than halving batch size (Table 2). The authors conclude extra compute should go mainly to model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a fixed time budget, larger models trained for fewer steps reach lower loss than smaller models trained longer.

record.problems: The authors identify the small pre-training data set and lack of hyperparameter tuning as limitations. The study uses a restricted set of down-scaled systems and does not fit power laws. Several validation-loss comparisons are presented only in plots or described qualitatively.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix C Tables 5 and 6 also report individual GLUE task metrics; the catalog retains the main GLUE-Large metric. Section 5.4 and Table 2 compare step count and batch size, but do not test the fixed-compute optimal parameter/token allocation in V3. Other GLUE values from Tables 3 and 4 were not added because the main size-sweep values and the table 1 shape comparisons are already represented.

untested.parts: Power-law form, any exponent, several orders of magnitude of loss scaling, and token or compute scaling.
FLOP-based compute-optimal parameter/token split and its exponent. The study's time-budget comparison is noted under fits_no_version.
Shape effects on loss above ~3.5M parameters. Shape effects with a quantified magnitude inside Kaplan's aspect-ratio range at larger scale.
Sizes above 41.6M, tasks beyond GLUE-Large/SST-2/CoLA, and any fitted predictive law.

missing.what: Validation loss across nine shapes at ~0.39M parameters (5.66 to 6.62), plus GLUE-Large for the top three
Final validation loss 3.24 (A=2), 3.29 (A=4) at 7.08M and 3.13 at 10.6M; GLUE 78.6/78.9/79.4
GLUE-Large 80.7 (20.6M) and 81.4 (41.6M) for compound-scaled BERT-style systems

record.verdict_notes: No power-law fits anywhere, so V1 rows are cannot_determine rather than supports. V4 rests on Table 7 (not in the rows) and the figure-only r2. Table 7 uses tiny models and extreme aspect ratios, so it may not generalise. The paper's GLUE-similarity-across-shapes claim (Observation 4) concerns downstream scores, not loss, and so is not V4 evidence. Training was on a single small corpus without hyperparameter tuning.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports validation loss for limited, relatively small model-size sweeps, but does not fit or test a power-law form, test several orders of magnitude, or independently vary tokens and compute.
No test of whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token counts or fitted growth powers. Step and batch comparisons do not establish the loss-minimising split.
The validation-loss shape comparisons are limited to the architectures and sizes studied; the paper does not quantify the size of shape effects across a wide range of model scales.
No other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning scaling laws, or transfer-law fits.
The study measures GLUE-Large on selected tasks and reports validation-loss comparisons, but does not establish a general predictive law for downstream tasks.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, data, or schedules; no test for curves bending away from a power law.

rows.operation_detail: Compared validation-loss curves for different model sizes over wall-clock time.
rows.measure: WikiText-103 validation loss over wall-clock time
rows.baseline: 3.5M-parameter model; approximately 11,800 seconds to the comparison point
rows.value: The larger system has lower validation loss at any measured point in time; its training time is approximately 14,400 seconds.
rows.note: The paper describes this as approximately doubling model parameters while increasing training time from approximately 11,800 to approximately 14,400 seconds. It does not fit a power law.
rows.check: Two sizes (3.5M vs 7.1M) that also differ in shape cannot show a power-law form, only the direction. The 'baseline' given is a training time (~11,800 s), not a loss value.

relationships.condition: Very small BERT-style models (~0.39M params) trained on WikiText-103 short sequences
relationships.reason: Based on the text, Table 7 (no row records it). At ~equal size, validation loss ranges 5.66 (L=2,H=128) to 6.62 (L=14–16), and it is 6.34 already at L=3,H=104. These are not slight differences. Shape direction also differs in r2.
relationships.display_finding: At approximately 0.39M parameters, validation loss ranged from 5.66 with 2 layers and width 128 to 6.62 with 14–16 layers, reaching 6.34 with 3 layers and width 104.

source_check.condition: Very small BERT-style models (~0.39M params) trained on WikiText-103 short sequences
source_check.reason: Table 7 gives losses 5.66–6.62 across approximately equal-size shapes, qualifying shape insensitivity in this tiny-model regime. These numerical results are not captured by r2, which concerns approximately 3.5M parameters.

relationships.condition: BERT-style width, depth and joint scaling
relationships.reason: GLUE-Large rises steadily with size: 65.4→72.3 (width) and 65.4→75.9 (depth), r14–r17 and r29–r33. Joint scaling gives 77.1→78.6 (r6). Table 4 adds 80.7 and 81.4 at 20.6M and 41.6M (text).
relationships.display_finding: GLUE-Large increased 65.4→72.3 with width, 65.4→75.9 with depth, and 77.1→78.6 with joint scaling; additional models scored 80.7 at 20.6M and 81.4 at 41.6M parameters.
